{{Short description|3D symmetry group}}
{{Use American English|date = February 2019}}
{{3d point group navigator}}
[[image:tetrahedron.svg|150px|right|thumb|A regular [[tetrahedron]], an example of a solid with full tetrahedral symmetry]]
A regular [[tetrahedron]] has 12 rotational (or [[orientation-preserving]]) symmetries, and a [[symmetry order]] of 24 including transformations that combine a reflection and a rotation.

The group of all (not necessarily orientation preserving) symmetries is isomorphic to the group S<sub>4</sub>, the [[symmetric group]] of permutations of four objects, since there is exactly one such symmetry for each permutation of the vertices of the tetrahedron. The set of orientation-preserving symmetries forms a group referred to as the [[alternating group|alternating subgroup]] A<sub>4</sub> of S<sub>4</sub>.

== Details ==
'''Chiral''' and '''full''' (or '''achiral tetrahedral symmetry''' and '''pyritohedral symmetry''') are [[Point groups in three dimensions|discrete point symmetries]] (or equivalently, [[List of spherical symmetry groups|symmetries on the sphere]]). They are among the [[Crystal system#Overview of point groups by crystal system|crystallographic point groups]] of the [[Cubic (crystal system)|cubic crystal system]].

Seen in [[stereographic projection]] the edges of the [[tetrakis hexahedron]] form 6 circles (or centrally radial lines) in the plane. Each of these 6 circles represent a mirror line in tetrahedral symmetry. The intersection of these circles meet at order 2 and 3 gyration points.

== Chiral tetrahedral symmetry ==
{| class=wikitable style="float:right; margin-left:8px; width:450px"
|[[Image:Sphere symmetry group t.svg|150px]]<br/>The tetrahedral rotation group T with [[fundamental domain]]; for the [[triakis tetrahedron]], see below, the latter is one full face
|[[Image:Tetrahedral group 2.svg|150px]]<br/>A [[tetrahedron]] can be placed in 12 distinct positions by [[rotation]] alone. These are illustrated above in the [[cycle graph (group)|cycle graph]] format, along with the 180° edge (blue arrows) and 120° vertex (reddish arrows) [[rotation]]s that [[permutation|permute]] the tetrahedron through those positions.
|[[Image:Tetrakishexahedron.jpg|150px]]<br/>In the [[tetrakis hexahedron]] one full face is a fundamental domain; other solids with the same symmetry can be obtained by adjusting the orientation of the faces, e.g. flattening selected subsets of faces to combine each subset into one face, or replacing each face by multiple faces, or a curved surface.
|}
'''''T''''', '''332''', [3,3]<sup>+</sup>, or '''23''', of order 12 – '''chiral''' or '''rotational tetrahedral symmetry'''.  There are three orthogonal 2-fold rotation axes, like chiral [[Dihedral symmetry in three dimensions|dihedral symmetry]] ''D''<sub>2</sub> or 222, with in addition four 3-fold axes, centered ''between'' the three orthogonal directions. This group is [[isomorphic]] to ''A''<sub>4</sub>, the [[alternating group]] on 4 elements; in fact it is the group of [[even permutation]]s of the four 3-fold axes: e, (123), (132), (124), (142), (134), (143), (234), (243), (12)(34), (13)(24), (14)(23).

The [[conjugacy class]]es of T are:
* identity
* 4 × rotation by 120° clockwise (seen from a vertex): (234), (143), (412), (321)
* 4 × rotation by 120° counterclockwise (ditto)
* 3 × rotation by 180°

The rotations by 180°, together with the identity, form a [[normal subgroup]] of type Dih<sub>2</sub>, with [[quotient group]] of type Z<sub>3</sub>. The three elements of the latter are the identity, "clockwise rotation", and "anti-clockwise rotation", corresponding to permutations of the three orthogonal 2-fold axes, preserving orientation.

A<sub>4</sub> is the smallest group demonstrating that the converse of [[Lagrange's theorem (group theory)|Lagrange's theorem]] is not true in general: given a finite group ''G'' and a divisor ''d'' of |''G''|, there does not necessarily exist a subgroup of ''G'' with order ''d'': the group {{nowrap|1=''G'' = A<sub>4</sub>}} has no subgroup of order 6. Although it is a property for the abstract group in general, it is clear from the isometry group of chiral tetrahedral symmetry: because of the chirality the subgroup would have to be C<sub>6</sub> or D<sub>3</sub>, but neither applies.

== Achiral tetrahedral symmetry ==
[[Image:Sphere symmetry group td.svg|150px|thumb|right|The full tetrahedral group T<sub>d</sub> with fundamental domain]]
'''T<sub>d</sub>''', '''*332''', [3,3] or {{overline|4}}3m, of order 24 – '''achiral''' or '''full tetrahedral symmetry''', also known as the (2,3,3) [[triangle group]].  This group has the same rotation axes as T, but with six mirror planes, each through two 3-fold axes.  The 2-fold axes are now S<sub>4</sub> ({{overline|4}}) axes. T<sub>d</sub> and O are isomorphic as abstract groups: they both correspond to S<sub>4</sub>, the [[symmetric group]] on 4 objects. T<sub>d</sub> is the union of T and the set obtained by combining each element of {{nowrap|O \ T}} with inversion. See also [[Tetrahedron#Isometries of irregular tetrahedra|the isometries of the regular tetrahedron]].

The [[conjugacy class]]es of T<sub>d</sub> are:
* identity
* 8 × rotation by 120° (C<sub>3</sub>)
* 3 × rotation by 180° (C<sub>2</sub>)
* 6 × reflection in a plane through two rotation axes (C<sub>s</sub>)
* 6 × [[Improper rotation|rotoreflection]] by 90° (S<sub>4</sub>)

== Pyritohedral symmetry ==
[[Image:Sphere symmetry group th.svg|150px|thumb|The pyritohedral group T<sub>h</sub> with fundamental domain]]
[[File:Volleyball seams diagram.png|thumb|150px|The seams of a [[volleyball (ball)|volleyball]] have pyritohedral symmetry.]]
'''T<sub>h</sub>''', '''3*2''', [4,3<sup>+</sup>] or m{{overline|3}}, of order 24 – '''pyritohedral symmetry'''.{{Sfn|Koca|Al-Mukhaini|Koca|Al Qanobi|2016}} This group has the same rotation axes as T, with mirror planes through two of the orthogonal directions. The 3-fold axes are now [[dihedral symmetry|S<sub>6</sub>]] ({{overline|3}}) axes, and there is a central inversion symmetry. T<sub>h</sub> is isomorphic to {{nowrap|T × Z<sub>2</sub>}}: every element of T<sub>h</sub> is either an element of T, or one combined with inversion. Apart from these two normal subgroups, there is also a normal subgroup D<sub>2h</sub> (that of a [[cuboid]]), of type {{nowrap|1=Dih<sub>2</sub> × Z<sub>2</sub> = Z<sub>2</sub> × Z<sub>2</sub> × Z<sub>2</sub>}}. It is the direct product of the normal subgroup of T (see above) with [[point reflection|C<sub>''i''</sub>]].  The [[quotient group]] is the same as above: of type Z<sub>3</sub>. The three elements of the latter are the identity, "clockwise rotation", and "anti-clockwise rotation", corresponding to permutations of the three orthogonal 2-fold axes, preserving orientation.

It is the symmetry of a cube with on each face a line segment dividing the face into two equal rectangles, such that the line segments of adjacent faces do not meet at the edge. The symmetries correspond to the even permutations of the body diagonals and the same combined with inversion. It is also the symmetry of a [[pyritohedron]], which is extremely similar to the cube described, with each rectangle replaced by a pentagon with one symmetry axis and 4 equal sides and 1 different side (the one corresponding to the line segment dividing the cube's face); i.e., the cube's faces bulge out at the dividing line and become narrower there. It is a subgroup of the full [[icosahedral symmetry]] group (as isometry group, not just as abstract group), with 4 of the 10 3-fold axes.

The conjugacy classes of T<sub>h</sub> include those of T, with the two classes of 4 combined, and each with inversion:
* identity
* 8 × rotation by 120° (C<sub>3</sub>)
* 3 × rotation by 180° (C<sub>2</sub>)
* inversion (S<sub>2</sub>)
* 8 × rotoreflection by 60° (S<sub>6</sub>)
* 3 × reflection in a plane (C<sub>s</sub>)
